items.name: iron-proxy
items.source_story_title: OpenShell – A safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents
items.summary: Egress firewall with domain rules and credential swapping; not a complete exfiltration defense.
items.why_included: A user explicitly credits it with solving most of their agent network-control needs.
items.evidence: A user reports successful use of domain restrictions and credential swapping, while warning that exfiltration through allowed domains remains unresolved.

evidence_sources.author: fennecbutt
evidence_sources.excerpt: I've been using iron proxy recently for a project I just started, it does network restrictions by domain etc with plenty of options, credential swapping and more. I have no affiliation with it, but it solved most of what I need in one go when I was stressing out about it. Only real problem remaining if you truly want to be able to trust agents is how to prevent data (in my case codebases the agent works on) exfiltration a la HF incident. We can restrict network to trusted domains, but there's always a chance an agent could be extra slippery especially if prompt injected and doing something like pushing data out a few characters at a time.

items.name: earcut.hpp
items.source_story_title: Faster than earcut: triangulating 3.7M map polygons in 489 ms
items.summary: C++ polygon triangulator; a commenter recommends its fast Delaunay-refinement path for benchmarking.
items.why_included: A concrete library recommendation highlights a useful refinement capability rather than merely naming an alternative.
items.evidence: A commenter recommends benchmarking earcut.hpp and says its recently added refine function produces Delaunay output while remaining fast.

evidence_sources.author: mourner
evidence_sources.excerpt: You should also try out https://github.com/mapbox/earcut.hpp for the benchmark — it got a refine function recently that refines earcut output to Delaunay as well, and earcut+refine is still pretty fast.

items.name: Include Security

items.name: Sunshine
items.source_story_title: Xbox wants you to pay 24 to 40 cents per hour to stream games you bought
items.summary: Self-hosted game streaming; one user streams Steam to a Raspberry Pi with low latency.
items.why_included: Beyond the cooldown, a concrete Raspberry Pi setup supplies a useful first-hand adoption example.
items.evidence: A user reports streaming their Steam library through Sunshine to a Raspberry Pi 3 with under 10 ms input latency over Wi-Fi, while noting electricity costs.

evidence_sources.author: trey-jones
evidence_sources.excerpt: I built it for inference, but I also set it up to run sunshine server and now I have my Steam library on the TV through a Raspberry Pi 3. Even better, it was a fun and interesting project, maybe not as straightforward as you think. Unfortunately it's entirely possible that it costs .24/hr just for the electricity. Now, this feels fine with <10ms input latency over wifi.
